scenario: WIBTA for declining to be a groomsman in a close friends wedding? | A friend I’ve known for about 10 years or so is getting married next month, and invited me out to dinner to “catch up” since it had been about a year since we hung out last. We chatted over dinner and after a while he asked me if I liked Kershaw knives. We’re both pretty outdoorsy and dabble a bit in the prepper life so it wasn’t an odd question to ask, and I responded with yes. He then slid a knife to me and asked me to check it out. I open it up and check out the craftsmanship, noticing an engraving on the blade. It was engraved with “ *lastname’s* wedding : 4-25-20 - Groomsman” and he had a big smile on his face when he saw I noticed it. He then asked me excitedly to be a groomsman for his wedding. Some additional context before getting into this next part. I’m the one who set him up with his fiancé, who happens to be very close friends to my ex, and you can kinda see where this is going. My ex was very mentally and emotionally abusive to me over a long period of time. It took me a while to realize it and I dumped her 2 years ago with no contact afterward at all. She is going to be a bridesmaid in their wedding and I’m not sure I want to put myself in that environment. Would I be the asshole for declining to be a part of their wedding? He asked me so last minute and I feel like it would mean a lot for me to be there for him and his soon-to-be wife.

prediction.raw: This is a complex and deeply personal situation, and there’s no universally "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends entirely on what feels sustainable and healthy for *you*. That said, I’d argue that **declining in this case is not only understandable but potentially necessary for your well-being**, and doing so wouldn’t make you "the asshole." Here’s why: ### **Why Declining Could Be the Right Choice (Score: 1)** 1. **Your Mental Health Comes First** - You’ve already endured years of emotional abuse from your ex, and being in close proximity to her—especially in a high-stress, celebratory environment like a wedding—could trigger anxiety, discomfort, or even retraumatization. Your friend’s excitement doesn’t negate the fact that this situation might be emotionally taxing for you. **Your peace is valid.** - If you’ve already established no contact with your ex, being at the wedding (even as a groomsman) could feel like a violation of your boundaries, especially if she’s a bridesmaid. It might feel like you’re being forced into a role where you’d have to interact with her or witness her happiness in a way that’s hard for you. 2. **The Invitation Was Last-Minute and Unprepared** - He presented this as a surprise ("check out this knife!"), which suggests he might not have fully considered the emotional weight of your history with his fiancée. That’s not your fault to navigate alone. **You’re not obligated to drop everything for a last-minute request, especially one tied to a person who’s caused you pain.** 3. **You’re Not the Only Support He Needs** - While it would mean a lot to him, you’re not his only friend. There are likely others who’d be happy to step in (or even other groomsmen who could share the role). His excitement shouldn’t pressure you into a decision that feels wrong for you. **His happiness shouldn’t come at your expense.** 4. **You Set Him Up with His Fiancée** - While that’s a kind gesture, it doesn’t mean you owe him anything further. You’ve already given him a huge gift by introducing them—now it’s his turn to show gratitude in a way that doesn’t harm you. **You’re not in debt to him emotionally.** 5. **The Groomsman Role Isn’t Just About the Wedding** - If you decline, you’re not saying you don’t care about his wedding—you’re saying you can’t be part of it in that specific way. You could still attend as a guest, send a heartfelt gift, or even help with other aspects of the planning (if it feels manageable). **Your absence as a groomsman doesn’t mean you’re absent from his life.** --- ### **Why You Might Feel Guilty (And Why That’s Okay)** - **He’s Your Friend:** It’s natural to feel bad for disappointing someone you care about, especially when he’s clearly excited. But guilt isn’t a valid reason to do something that harms you. - **You Set Him Up:** You might feel like you "owe" him for that. But relationships aren’t transactional—you’re not obligated to repay kindness with more kindness if it’s not sustainable. - **Fear of Being "The Bad Guy":** You’re worried he’ll think you’re being selfish or ungrateful. But if you explain your reasons (even briefly), he might understand. Many people would rather have a friend who’s honest about their limits than one who forces themselves into a role that’s not right for them. --- ### **How to Handle It (If You Decide to Decline)** If you choose to say no, you can be kind but firm. Here’s a script that keeps it warm but clear: > *"I really appreciate you thinking of me for this—it means a lot that you’d want me to be part of your big day. But after talking about it, I realized I’m not in a place where I could be a groomsman without feeling uncomfortable. I don’t want to be the reason you’re disappointed, so I think it’s best if I’m just a guest. I hope you understand, and I’ll still be there to celebrate with you!"* This: - Acknowledges his feelings. - Stays honest about your limits. - Doesn’t over-explain (you don’t owe him a detailed breakdown of your past). - Leaves the door open for friendship to continue. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (It’s the Right Choice for You)** This isn’t about being "the asshole"—it’s about being someone who prioritizes their own well-being. You’re not responsible for managing his emotions or your ex’s presence. **Your mental health and comfort matter more than any wedding role.** That said, if you *do* decide to attend as a guest, make sure you have a plan to protect yourself (e.g., sitting far from your ex, having an exit strategy, or even bringing a friend for support). But declining isn’t wrong—it’s self-respect in action. Would you feel differently if you knew your ex wouldn’t be there? Or if you had more time to process it? Sometimes the answer changes with perspective.
